stories.headline: US-IRAN DEAL ON VERGE OF SIGNING — OIL DROPS 2% AS HORMUZ REOPENING PRICED IN
stories.body: Trump announced a European signing ceremony Friday after Iran submitted a final draft agreement, effectively ending months of conflict that shut the Strait of Hormuz. WTI crude fell over 2% to $85.65 — its lowest in nearly two months — as traders priced in the pending release of an estimated 100 million barrels of stranded tanker cargo once the Strait reopens.
stories.explain: The Iran-oil link runs through the geopolitical risk premium: economists estimated Hormuz's closure added $15–25 per barrel to WTI above the supply-demand equilibrium price, and today's 2%+ drop is the market front-running the collapse of that premium well before a single new Iranian barrel flows. The strategic relevance for next week's Fed meeting is direct — May CPI came in at 4.2% YoY with energy accounting for over 60% of the monthly gain, and a sustained oil decline to $82–85 would mechanically subtract roughly 0.8–1.0 percentage point from annualized headline CPI, giving the Fed disinflation it didn't have to manufacture through rate hikes. This is the mechanism that pushed the September cut probability from 48% Thursday to 62% Friday — not optimism, but an arithmetic improvement in the inflation path.

stories.headline: SPACEX PRICES HISTORY'S LARGEST-EVER IPO AT $75B — SPCX SURGES 20% IN NASDAQ DEBUT
stories.body: SpaceX raised $75 billion at $135 per share in the largest IPO in history, trading under SPCX on the Nasdaq. Shares opened at $150 and hit a session high of $168.75 (+25%), valuing the company above $2 trillion and making Elon Musk the world's first individual trillionaire. The Nasdaq 100 gained 0.59% while the broader Nasdaq Composite fell as the IPO diverted capital from existing positions.
stories.explain: Funding a $75B IPO requires buyers to come up with $75B in cash, which means liquidating existing equity — that selling pressure explains why the Nasdaq Composite fell even as the NDX held up, since SPCX won't join the Nasdaq 100 until the September quarterly rebalance. The more durable market structure story is what happens at that rebalance: once SPCX clears float and profitability screens for S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 inclusion, passive index funds face mandatory buying at any price — a known, scheduled demand event that typically creates 'pre-inclusion drift' as active traders front-run the forced flow weeks in advance, creating a potential second leg of appreciation for the stock.

stories.headline: MAY CPI HITS 4.2%, A THREE-YEAR HIGH — BUT CORE RUNS SOFTER THAN EXPECTED AT +2.9%
stories.body: The May Consumer Price Index (released Wednesday June 10) rose 0.5% MoM and 4.2% YoY — the highest annual rate since April 2023 — with energy accounting for over 60% of the monthly gain (+3.9% MoM, +23.5% YoY). Core CPI came in at +0.2% MoM (below the 0.3% estimate) and +2.9% YoY. Shelter inflation decelerated sharply to +0.3% MoM from April's +0.6%.
stories.explain: The split between a hot headline and a soft core tells the entire story: May's 4.2% CPI is almost entirely an energy problem, not a broad demand problem. Core at +2.9% and shelter decelerating toward +3.4% YoY are consistent with the Fed's disinflation thesis for non-energy components. What makes today's Iran deal transformative is that it attacks exactly the driver making headline CPI dangerous: if WTI settles at $82–85 through summer, energy makes a large negative contribution to June and July CPI prints, potentially pulling headline inflation back below 3.5% within two months — the scenario the bond market began pricing Friday afternoon.

stories.headline: UMICH CONSUMER SENTIMENT REBOUNDS TO 48.9 IN JUNE — FIRST INCREASE SINCE JANUARY
stories.body: The preliminary June University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment index rose to 48.9 from 44.8 in May, the first monthly increase since January, with improvement broad-based across age, income, and party affiliation. Year-ahead inflation expectations eased from 4.8% to 4.6%; 5–10 year expectations fell more meaningfully from 3.9% to 3.4%. The index remains 19% below year-ago levels.
stories.explain: The Fed watches the 5–10 year inflation expectation as a canary for whether elevated near-term inflation is becoming structurally embedded in wage demands and pricing behavior — the precondition for a wage-price spiral. The drop from 3.9% to 3.4% today reduces that risk materially: workers demanding 4%+ wages because they expect 4%+ inflation is a self-fulfilling dynamic the Fed would have to break with aggressive hikes. That said, 3.4% sits well above the Fed's implicit comfort zone of 2.2–2.5%, so the direction is encouraging but the level still argues for hold, not cut — it's a yellow light dialing back from red.

stories.headline: FED MEETS NEXT WEEK — HOLD CERTAIN BUT DOT PLOT SIGNALS WHETHER SEPTEMBER CUT IS LIVE
stories.body: The Federal Reserve holds its June FOMC meeting next week with a rate decision expected Wednesday June 17. A hold is universally priced in, but the quarterly dot plot is the real market event: traders want to know whether the median member still sees at least one 25 bps cut in 2026 or has pushed easing to 2027. Markets now price 62% odds of a September cut, up from 48% Thursday, on the Iran deal and softer core CPI.
stories.explain: The dot plot functions as a commitment device: anonymous committee member forecasts shift market expectations without an actual policy move. The critical threshold is whether the median 2026 dot holds at the March projection of one cut. With energy-driven CPI now facing a direct supply catalyst (Iran normalization) and core running below consensus at 2.9%, at least two or three members who were previously on the fence may pencil in a September move. If the 2026 median still shows one cut, the 62% September probability stays anchored; if the median shifts to zero, expect 2-year yields to jump 10–15 bps immediately and rate-sensitive sectors — REITs, utilities, homebuilders — to sell off hard.

stories.headline: KNICKS ERASE 29-POINT HALFTIME DEFICIT IN GAME 4, LEAD NBA FINALS 3-1; GAME 5 SATURDAY
stories.body: New York erased a 29-point halftime deficit — the largest comeback in NBA Finals history — to defeat San Antonio 107-106 in Game 4 on OG Anunoby's tip-in with 1.2 seconds remaining. Jalen Brunson led all scorers with 36 points; Anunoby added 33. The Knicks lead the series 3-1 and are one win from their first NBA championship since 1973. Game 5 is Saturday night in San Antonio.

stories.headline: MAHOMES EXTENDED THROUGH 2033 FOR $504.75M AS SEAHAWKS HOST SUPER BOWL RING CEREMONY
stories.body: Kansas City added two years to Patrick Mahomes' contract, now running through 2033 at a total value of $504.75 million. The Seahawks completed mandatory minicamp this week and hosted their Super Bowl LX ring ceremony, celebrating February's 29-13 win over New England. First-round pick Jadarian Price signed, making Seattle's entire 2026 draft class under contract.

stories.headline: UW HUSKIES LAND 3-STAR EDGE CHAZ GRAY OVER TENNESSEE, CLEMSON, AND OHIO STATE
stories.body: Washington secured a commitment from Chaz Gray, a 3-star edge rusher from St. Joseph Regional HS in New Jersey ranked No. 33 nationally at his position by 247Sports. Gray chose UW over Tennessee, Clemson, and Ohio State — the Huskies' 18th commit in the 2027 recruiting class. Earlier in June, 4-star WR Tre Moore from Texas also committed to Washington over Ohio State and Miami.

stories.headline: SUMMER RECRUITING HEATS UP — PROGRAMS FINALIZING ROSTERS AHEAD OF JULY EVALUATION PERIOD
stories.body: With the spring transfer portal window closed, programs are locking in final roster spots before July. Washington Basketball hired former Marquette assistant DeAndre Haynes and added Texas Tech transfer LaJuan Watts, who joins his brother DeSean on the Husky roster. 2026 local prospect Lattimore Ford (Mount Si HS) is also committed to UW as Sprinkle continues rebuilding the roster.

deepDive.title: The Geopolitical Risk Premium in Oil — How Hormuz Priced Into Crude and What the Unwind Means for the Fed
content: WTI crude fell over 2% today to $85.65 as the US-Iran peace deal moved to its signing stage. The surface-level explanation — more supply equals lower prices — is obvious. The analytically interesting questions are: how did futures markets price the *possibility* of supply disruption months before resolution, why does the 2% drop today understate the eventual normalization, and why is the Iran peace deal likely the single most important input for next week's Federal Reserve decision?

A geopolitical risk premium is the per-barrel surcharge embedded in spot prices to compensate traders for the probability that supply gets disrupted. When Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz — taking roughly 20% of global seaborne oil offline — economists estimated the closure added $15–25 per barrel to WTI above the supply-demand equilibrium price. The mechanism is probabilistic: traders don't assume the closure is permanent; they apply a discount rate to the probability distribution of when supply normalizes. As the deal moved from rumored to likely to imminent, each step compressed that probability premium. Today's 2%+ move is front-running the remaining probability — markets aren't waiting for Iranian crude to actually flow before deflating the last $10–15 of premium.

The wrinkle most observers underestimate is the shadow inventory problem. During the Strait closure, an estimated 100 million barrels accumulated in tankers unable to transit — a floating armada. Historical precedent from the Gulf of Mexico reopening after Hurricane Katrina (2005) is instructive: crude fell approximately 8% in the first two weeks post-reopening not because demand dropped, but because the accumulated inventory created temporary oversupply even though underlying conditions were unchanged. The Iran situation is two to three times larger in volume. Traders who bought crude futures as a disruption hedge are now incentivized to sell *before* that supply wall hits markets — amplifying today's decline. Risk premiums don't decay linearly; they collapse as the settlement event approaches a known date.

For Fed positioning: May CPI hit 4.2% YoY, with energy accounting for over 60% of the monthly gain. If WTI settles at $82–85 through summer, the energy component of headline CPI makes a large *negative* contribution to June and July prints, potentially pulling headline inflation from 4.2% back toward 3.0–3.5% within two months — without a single rate hike. Watch the 5-year breakeven inflation rate (currently ~2.8%): if it drops toward 2.5% on oil normalization over the next two weeks, the bond market will reprice a September cut regardless of what the dot plot says Wednesday. Geopolitics just became the most important variable in U.S. monetary policy — and a $15-per-barrel risk premium unwinding is doing the Fed's work for it.
